title: Composite Key Order: Equality Before Range
description: Column order in a composite index decides whether a range predicate can seek; equality column first, range column second. Why it matters: composite index design is a fundamental, everyday DBA/developer skill -- getting column order wrong is one of the most common indexing mistakes.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

This lesson is about a detail that trips up almost every developer the first time they build a multi-column ("composite") index: the *order* you list the columns in matters enormously, and getting it backwards can silently make an index far less useful than you'd expect — even though technically "the index exists and contains the right columns."

Here's the setup: the query is `WHERE CustomerId = 100 AND OrderDate >= '2024-10-01'`, and there's a composite index built as `(OrderDate, CustomerId)` that even happens to include every other column the query needs. On paper this looks like it should be a great index — it has both filter columns and covers the query — but the plan still does far more reads than it should, close to what you'd expect from scanning a big chunk of the table.

To understand why, picture a composite index the way you'd picture a phone book sorted first by city, then by last name within each city. If you want "everyone named Smith in any city," that sorted-by-city-first phone book doesn't help you much — the Smiths are scattered across every city section, so you'd have to check every city's pages to gather all of them. But if you want "everyone in Chicago," that same phone book is perfect — you jump straight to the Chicago section and you're done. The order of the sort determines what kind of question the structure is good at answering.

That's exactly the situation in this lesson. The index `(OrderDate, CustomerId)` is sorted first by date, and *within* each date, by customer. Your query has an **equality** condition on `CustomerId` (`= 100`, one exact value) and a **range** condition on `OrderDate` (`>= '2024-10-01'`, an open-ended range of many possible dates). Because the index is sorted date-first, SQL Server can seek to the right starting date easily — but from that starting point onward, it has to scan through the index entries for *every date* in the range, checking each one to see if `CustomerId` happens to be 100, because customer 100's rows aren't grouped together — they're scattered across many different date "buckets," one per day they ordered. That's a lot of unnecessary work: essentially scanning most of the recent-date range and filtering out non-matching customers row by row, rather than jumping directly to just customer 100's rows.

The fix is to flip the column order: build the index as `(CustomerId, OrderDate)` instead. Now the index is sorted first by customer, and *within* each customer, sorted by date. SQL Server can seek directly to the block of entries belonging to customer 100 (using the equality predicate to jump straight there, exactly like flipping to the right city in the phone book), and *within* that customer's block, the rows are already sorted by date — so the range condition (`OrderDate >= '2024-10-01'`) can be applied as a simple, cheap scan through an already-tiny, already-sorted subset. Total cost: a handful of reads, instead of scanning through a big date range across every customer.

This gives you a genuinely universal rule for building composite indexes, one that applies basically everywhere, not just in SQL Server: **put your equality columns first, and your range columns last.** Equality conditions (`= something`) narrow things down precisely and can be seeked directly — you want them leading the index so the engine can jump straight to the relevant slice. Range conditions (`>=`, `<=`, `BETWEEN`, `>`, `<`) can only usefully "take over" scanning *after* the equality columns have already narrowed things down, because once you're inside a range comparison, the sort order can't help you skip around anymore — you're committed to scanning forward or backward through that range. If you put a range column before an equality column in your composite key, you get exactly the problem shown in this lesson: the equality condition becomes useless for seeking, because it's buried inside a wide range instead of being the entry point.

Why does this matter day to day? Composite indexes are extremely common — almost any query filtering on more than one column benefits from one — and this exact mistake (accidentally leading with the range column) is one of the most frequent index-design errors developers make, especially when the index was originally built for a *different* query that happened to filter differently. Once you internalize "equality first, range last," you'll be able to look at almost any WHERE clause and know immediately what column order a supporting composite index should use.

It helps to practice this rule on a few quick examples until it becomes automatic. Suppose you're querying "all logins for user 42 in the last 7 days" — `UserId = 42` is equality, `LoginTime >= ...` is a range, so the index should be `(UserId, LoginTime)`, user first. Suppose instead you're querying "all logins across any user between two specific timestamps, for an audit report" — there's no equality condition at all here, just a range, so the "equality first" rule doesn't really apply and a simple index on `LoginTime` alone might be the better fit. The rule isn't a rigid formula to memorize blindly — it's a reflection of how a sorted structure actually behaves: equality conditions can jump straight to one narrow slice, and only within an already-narrow slice does scanning through a range become cheap. If you ever find yourself unsure which order to use, it can help to literally sketch out (on paper, or in your head) what the sorted list would look like under each ordering, and ask which one lets you jump to the smallest possible starting point for your specific query. This kind of mental simulation — "if I sorted the data this way, could I jump straight to what I need, or would I have to check a lot of irrelevant entries along the way?" — is genuinely the core skill behind almost all index design, not just this one lesson.

A closing thought: this rule also explains why a single, unchanging index sometimes needs to become two separate indexes over time. If your application develops a second common query that filters primarily by date instead of by customer, no single composite index can serve both patterns optimally -- you may need a second, differently-ordered index alongside the first, accepting the small extra write cost in exchange for both query shapes staying fast.

## Scenario
`SELECT CustomerId, OrderDate, Total FROM Orders WHERE CustomerId = 100 AND OrderDate >= '2024-10-01'` is served by a composite index `IX_Orders_Date_Cust (OrderDate, CustomerId) INCLUDE (Total)`. The index even covers every column the query needs — yet it still does ~250 logical reads to return two dozen rows.

## Why it's slow
Column **order inside the key** matters. This index leads with `OrderDate`, a **range** predicate. SQL Server can seek to the start of `OrderDate >= '2024-10-01'`, but once inside that range the rows are *not* ordered by `CustomerId` — so `CustomerId = 100` becomes a **residual predicate**: the engine reads **every order in the date range** (across all 3000 customers) and throws away the ones that aren't customer 100.

## What to look for
- The plan is an **Index Seek**, but reads are far higher than the ~24 rows returned — a classic sign the seek is really a range scan with a residual filter.
- The equality column sits *after* a range column in the key.

## The concept
Order composite keys **equality columns first, range columns last**. Rebuild as `(CustomerId, OrderDate)`: now the seek jumps straight to `CustomerId = 100`, and because those rows *are* ordered by `OrderDate`, the `OrderDate >= …` range is a second seek on top — not a residual. Reads collapse from ~250 to ~3. (Both indexes INCLUDE `Total`, so this is purely about key order, not covering.)
startingQuery: SELECT CustomerId, OrderDate, Total FROM Orders WHERE CustomerId = 100 AND OrderDate >= '2024-10-01';
hints: The index covers every column, so covering isn't the problem -- look at the order of the two key columns.
A range predicate (OrderDate >=) leading the key means the equality (CustomerId =) can't be a seek; it's applied as a residual.
Rebuild the index as (CustomerId, OrderDate): equality column first, range column second.
